A specific neuron group (hDeltaH, hDeltaA, hDeltaI, hDeltaG) that appears to support navigation via fast synaptic weight updates rather than activation dynamics — a mechanism current language models do not have. This is a claim about circuits, made from the data, and testable; almost nothing in the viral section is.

This is fast-weight continual learning in a fly, something current LLMs don't do!

clusters.commentary: A fly connectome given a bicycle-balancing task, which the author says it failed 1,238 times before something changed, with no hand-written balance code. The improvement is the load-bearing claim and the thread does not show the learning rule that produced it.

items.author: @adamgrag
items.text: I GAVE A FLY BRAIN ONE TASK: LEARN TO BALANCE ON A BICYCLE. IT FELL 1,238 TIMES. THEN SOMETHING CHANGED. No instructions. No balance code.

clusters.title: A fly wandering through Pokemon Red
clusters.commentary: A fly connectome wired into Pokemon Red as a rate-based leaky-integrator network, with screen motion, Game Boy audio and wall collisions stimulating real visual, auditory and touch neurons, and button presses read off descending and motor activity. The author's framing is unusually careful: he notes that many builds plug a fine-tuned model into the fly rather than using the fly's own circuitry, and says plainly that his fly has no idea it is playing Pokemon.

items.title: I made a fly play Pokemon Red
items.author: Alex Xiao Cai
items.text: Inspired by Twitch Plays Pokemon, I made a fly play Pokemon Red. It uses the actual connectivity of a real fly connectome, simulated as a rate-based leaky-integrator network.

clusters.title: Two fly brains playing chess against each other
clusters.commentary: Two flies, each with a full copy of a 127,400-neuron connectome, playing chess with reward implemented as activating random parts of the brain and punishment as deactivating them. The author says the first version moved randomly and only began producing checkmates once a heuristic was added to nudge decisions, so the chess ability is substantially the heuristic's rather than the connectome's.

items.title: I made two virtual flies play chess with each other
items.author: Alex Xiao Cai
items.text: I decided to make two virtual flies play chess with each other. Each has its own full copy of the real 127,400-neuron connectome, its own memory of wins and losses, its own personality.

clusters.title: Music through the fly connectome, and a retraction
clusters.commentary: Audio pushed through the Janelia male CNS connectome as a leaky integrate-and-fire network, entering at 86 Johnston's organ afferents and leaving as MIDI from 56 descending neurons, with a companion video showing every neuron firing at its real anatomical position. Petkov then retracted half of his own headline result: the claim that signal is at chance two synapses in came from a single run, and across ten seeds the second-hop layer carries roughly 1-2% of the first hop's signal, detectable over ten runs but invisible in any one of them. The correction, not the music, is the most methodologically useful thing in this index.

items.title: Twenty seconds of music pushed through a fruit fly's connectome
items.author: Radoslav Petkov
items.text: The Janelia male CNS connectome, 165,122 neurons, 15 million synapses, simulated as a leaky integrate-and-fire network. Audio enters through 86 Johnston's organ afferents. Descending neuron firing rates come out as MIDI.

items.title: You can now watch it happen
items.author: Radoslav Petkov
items.text: Every dot in this video is a real neuron at its real position in the imaged animal, from Janelia's male Drosophila CNS volume: 165,122 traced neurons and roughly 15 million synaptic connections.

items.title: Half of it was wrong
items.author: Radoslav Petkov
items.text: The claim was that sound reaches the descending neurons across a single synapse, and that two synapses in the signal is at chance. That measurement ran once. Across ten seeds the two-synapse layer cleared significance in half the runs and missed in the other half.

clusters.title: A fly brain in Minecraft, trying to farm
clusters.commentary: A 34-minute build log rather than a clip: connectome output is wired into Minecraft through the creator's own mod and pointed at growing wheat, with the mod and training setup published as open source (FlyBridge). The title's claim that it 'learned to farm' is the creator's; the length of the video at least makes the surrounding training loop visible, which is where most of the behaviour in builds like this comes from.

items.title: I Put a Fly's Brain in Minecraft. It Learned to Farm.
items.author: SWOT

clusters.title: A fly brain playing Overwatch
clusters.commentary: 166,700 fly neurons mapped onto Overwatch inputs, with the creator picking Moira because, as he puts it, the fly does not need to aim - Moira does it for them. The post is unusually candid that the connectome ends up reduced to right-clicking, flanking and dying, which is closer to what these ports actually demonstrate than most of the wave admits.

items.author: @kenopsia_ow
items.text: I trained 166,700 fruit fly neurons to play Overwatch. It performed best on Moira. The fly doesn't need to aim, Moira does it for them. 166,700 neurons reduced to right clicking, flanking, dying, and ulting a Torb turret. Millions of years of evolution for this. Amazing.

clusters.title: A virtual world for a simulated fly, in the browser
clusters.commentary: An open-source browser environment that drops a simulated fruit fly into a generated world, and the widest-reaching item in this run at roughly 1.8 million views when collected. The author's framing - that observation is substrate-independent and the fly experiences the world as solid - is his philosophical position, not something the demo establishes.

items.author: @muellerberndt
items.text: I put a Cadence patchnet into a virtual fruit fly. This creates an actual fly matrix in your browser that the fly experiences as a solid world (observation is substrate-independent). All open-source, Github link on the page. floatingpragma.io/cadence-examples/fly-matrix/

clusters.title: A digitized fly brain conditioned with a simulated dopamine reward
clusters.commentary: A multi-day conditioning stunt on what the creator states is a 139,255-neuron digitized fly brain: a simulated dopamine pulse is tied to a lit cigarette, the fly reportedly learns within a day that the glowing stick means reward, and in the follow-up it repeatedly shocks a second fly to get one. The reward pathway and the second fly are both his own engineering, so what this shows is a hand-built reward loop changing behaviour in his simulation, not addiction latent in the connectome.

items.author: @adamgrag
items.text: I did something slightly evil to a digitized fly brain and now I feel bad. Two weeks ago I gave it a lit cigarette. Every puff fires a small dopamine pulse. It took the fly about a day to figure out that the glowing stick equals good feeling.

items.author: @adamgrag
items.text: this morning my fly had a best friend by 2pm it had shocked that friend eight times for a cigarette and it did the last one after standing at the button that would have set it free. quick recap for new people: this is a digitized fly brain, 139,255 neurons, that I got hooked on

clusters.commentary: A Friday Night Funkin' mod driven by a fly-brain model, released on GitHub and working across the main FNF engines. Worth noting against the rest of the wave: the creator states roughly 1,000-2,000 reconstructed MaleCNS circuit neurons, not the full 166,700-neuron connectome nearly every other post cites.

clusters.title: dotFly: the connectome simulated in Godot
clusters.commentary: The creator says he simulates the full 166,700-neuron connectome in real time inside Godot, with the fly flying around a virtual room, and that he built it to understand the Mario and Doom ports rather than to outdo them. Far less reach than the game ports, but aimed at the simulation itself instead of the stunt.

items.author: @konradkokosa
items.text: Everyone was making a fruit fly's brain play Mario or Doom last week. I had to build somethong on my own to understand what it is all about. So, meet dotFly - the full 166,700-neuron connectome, simulated in real time in @godotengine, flying around a virtual room looking for

clusters.title: A fly-brain NPC in Roblox
clusters.commentary: An unedited test of fly-brain NPC mechanics in Roblox, with a playable game published alongside it. Separate from the Roblox port already indexed here - different creator, different game, and framed as ongoing development rather than a finished result.

items.title: Roblox Fly Brain NPC (UNEDITED)
items.author: ExtraJackGuest

clusters.title: A fly brain playing the Chrome dino game
clusters.commentary: The Chrome dino game driven by the MaleCNS map, which the creator describes as giving the fly something fun to do - endless jumping. Her description also claims she has 'a real conscious fly running on my computer'; nothing in the 110-second clip bears on that, and the demonstrated behaviour is a single repeated action.

items.title: Fruit fly BRAIN plays the Dino Game
items.author: CyberAliceVT

clusters.title: A fly learning Flappy Bird through a dopamine signal
clusters.commentary: A Flappy Bird agent built on open connectome data with a dopamine-style reward signal, which the author says visibly improves from crashing immediately to clearing pipes on purpose over a few minutes. The improvement comes from that hand-built reward loop rather than from the wiring diagram, a distinction the post's 'its actual brain chemistry' framing blurs.

items.title: I built a fly that learns to play Flappy Bird
items.author: Narendra Naik
items.text: I spent the week building a fly that learns to play Flappy Bird using its actual brain chemistry, using the open-source fruit fly connectome data. It's inspired by how real fruit flies learn: a tiny brain region releases a dopamine signal every time something works or fails, and that reshapes the fly's decisions in real time.

clusters.title: What it would take to drive Unreal Engine 5 from the connectome
clusters.commentary: Not a build: an Unreal-focused channel walks through a proposed closed-loop architecture - engine to sensory encoder to neural simulation to motor decoder and back - for driving UE5 from the fly connectome, including why the simulation would run off the game thread. It cites more than 166,000 neurons and 125 million synapses for the MaleCNS release, and is explicit that the UE5 version does not exist yet.

items.title: A Fruit Fly Brain Is Playing Doom. Here's How It Could Control Unreal Engine 5
items.author: CodieFN | Unreal Engine

clusters.title: The fly brain as a running comedy bit
clusters.commentary: A comedy bit in an ongoing series - training an 'AI fly brain' to receive communion - rather than a technical build, and the model behind it is never specified. Indexed as a marker of how far the wave has travelled from the data release; it demonstrates nothing about the connectome.

items.author: @ParanoidAmerica
items.text: Training an AI fly brain to receive the Body and Blood of Christ so it can finally be saved after everyone in the comments said it was going to Hell.

items.author: DOENUT FACTORY

clusters.title: RadFly: the connectome as an X-ray classifier
clusters.commentary: A weekend research experiment from Mecha Health using the fruit fly connectome as the architecture of a neural network for chest X-ray classification, reported at over 0.80 AUROC for pleural effusion on a subset of MIMIC-CXR. The team says they deliberately used no external pretrained network so the fly 'can't cheat'; as with the knee-MRI build already indexed here, the comparison that would settle what the connectome contributes - a random graph of matched degree - is not reported.

items.title: Can a fly read X-rays? Actually, yes.
items.author: Nina Montana Brown
items.text: We built RadFly, a small research experiment using the fruit fly connectome as the basis of a neural network for medical image classification and trained the brain on a small subset of MIMIC-CXR. RadFly achieves an AUROC of over 80% on pleural effusion classification.

clusters.title: 165,122 neurons running on your own GPU, in the browser
clusters.commentary: A browser viewer that runs the male CNS wiring - 165,122 neurons by the author's count - in compute shaders on the visitor's own GPU, mapped onto a 3D fly, so escape, flight, grooming and feeding can each be traced to the neurons and muscles driving them. Built on the male CNS connectome, FlyWire, the Shiu et al. brain model and flybody, and credited as such; the post's 'nobody programmed those reactions' line understates the neuron-to-muscle mapping, which is engineering.

items.title: Fruit Fly: a real fruit fly's wiring map, running in your browser
items.author: Elbert P.
items.text: Fruit Fly is a real fruit fly's brain wiring with 165,122 neurons that is simulated with compute shaders and mapped to a 3D fly, so you can watch its neurons drive what it does. This site runs that map live on your own GPU in the local browser.

clusters.title: What the male connectome is, and what the game ports are not
clusters.commentary: An explainer on the MaleCNS release - 166,700 neurons and roughly 125 million synaptic connections, brain plus ventral nerve cord - and the Doom, Mario 64 and Beat Saber ports that followed within days. One of the few widely-shared posts to state plainly that a connectome is a wiring diagram rather than an upload, and that the Doom project's own documentation does not claim the fly learned to survive better over time.

items.title: Scientists mapped the male fruit fly CNS, then engineers connected it to Doom
items.author: Anna Simonova
items.author_title: Data Scientist | NLP Engineer | AI Engineer
items.text: It is important to be precise, though: this is a wiring diagram, not a literal upload of a fly's mind. A connectome tells us which neurons are connected, but it does not capture every electrical, chemical, and physiological detail of a living brain.

clusters.title: Virtual Fly Brain: where the data actually lives
clusters.commentary: A tour of Virtual Fly Brain as an access layer over the fly datasets - one anatomy ontology across every dataset and life stage, reachable from the browser, Python and R, an MCP endpoint and a chat interface. Infrastructure rather than a result, and the most direct answer in this index to where the connectome data comes from and how to query it.

items.title: Virtual Fly Brain: every fly connectome, image and gene in one place
items.author: Virtual Fly Brain

clusters.title: Every neuron in the male fly CNS, rendered
clusters.commentary: A nine-second 3D rendering of all neurons in the male fly brain and ventral nerve cord, published by the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology alongside the connectome and credited to Philipp Schlegel, with data from the Janelia FlyEM team, the Cambridge Connectomics Group, the MRC-LMB and Google Research. A visualization of the dataset, not a simulation running on it.

items.title: All neurons in the male fruit fly CNS
items.author: MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology

clusters.title: The optic lobe connectome, visualized
clusters.commentary: Janelia's visualization of the fruit fly optic lobe connectome, which they describe as mapping more than 50,000 neurons across more than 700 distinct types, showing the neuropils and some of the columnar neurons of the visual system. Predates the male CNS release by two years and is the sort of lab visualization the 2026 viral builds are layered on top of.

items.title: Columnar neurons from the Drosophila optic lobe
items.author: HHMI's Janelia Research Campus

items.title: A sample of neurons from the Drosophila optic lobe
items.author: HHMI's Janelia Research Campus

clusters.title: FlyWire's own overview of the female whole-brain wiring diagram
clusters.commentary: FlyWire's summary of the female whole-brain connectome, stating 127,000 neurons, 32 million synapses, four years of work and 2.7 million manual edits, with renders by the project itself. Useful as the baseline figure set that the 2026 posts are usually misquoting or conflating with the male CNS numbers.

items.title: FlyWire Overview and Data Types
items.author: FlyWire Princeton

clusters.title: Querying the connectome, concretely
clusters.commentary: A short demo of FlyWire's connectivity app: picking a cell, pulling its upstream and downstream partners, and visualizing primary neurotransmitters and key neuropils. The tooling that makes 'query the connectome' a specific operation rather than a slogan.

items.title: FlyWire Connectivity App Demo
items.author: FlyWire Princeton

clusters.title: The first auditory connectome, and wiring that predicted responses
clusters.commentary: A visualization accompanying Baker et al. in Current Biology (2022), described as the first auditory connectome in any system: synaptic connectivity among more than 500 neurons across both hemispheres, 24 newly identified cell types, and a non-hierarchical network rather than separate pathways per sound. FlyWire's summary states the wiring diagram was able to predict auditory responses, which makes this a concrete precedent for the claim the viral builds gesture at.

items.title: Drosophila Auditory Connectome
items.author: FlyWire Princeton

clusters.title: Hacking the Fly Connectome: a hands-on workshop
clusters.commentary: A 2021 Virtual Fly Brain workshop on querying and analysing fly connectomics across neuPrint, CATMAID and VFB, with interactive Python and R notebooks and exercises on finding neurons by type, location, connectivity and morphological similarity. Five years old and still the most practical item in this index for working with the data rather than watching it.

items.title: Virtual Fly Brain: Hacking the Fly Connectome Workshop 2021
items.author: Virtual Fly Brain

clusters.title: Flappy Bird flapped by the giant fiber escape neuron
clusters.commentary: A game port that actually names its mechanism: a 'danger approaching' signal is injected into the visual looming neurons, propagated through the male CNS wiring to DNp01 (the giant fiber that runs from brain to the jump and flight muscles), and the bird flaps when DNp01 fires. The author states nothing is trained and that 166,700 neurons are simulated per game frame. Naming the output neuron rather than just claiming 'the fly plays X' is what separates this from most of the game ports.

items.title: Can a Fruit Fly Brain Play Flappy Bird?
items.author: NoloWiz
Rupesh Sreeraman
items.text: I used male fruit fly brain mapping to play Flappy Bird. When the bird is about to fall, I send a 'danger approaching' signal into the fly's looming neurons ... to the giant fiber (DNp01). If the giant fiber fires, the bird flaps. This is not AI. Nothing is trained.

clusters.title: A whole fly brain on a 15-pound touchscreen
clusters.commentary: The published FlyWire whole-brain model (Shiu et al., Nature 2024) run on a GBP 15 ESP32 display with 520 KB of RAM: the author states 138,639 neurons and 15 million connections, with only the few thousand neurons actually firing held in memory, the wiring of the ~2,100 that ever fire in flash, and the remainder on an SD card. He says every run checked on the board matches a reference simulation's spikes. The achievement is memory engineering, not new biology.

items.title: I put a whole fruit-fly brain on a £15 touchscreen
items.author: Christian Graham

clusters.title: A simulated male CNS steering a physical rover
clusters.commentary: A real rover driven by a MaleCNS simulation: a hand rushed at the camera makes the escape circuit fire and the rover backs off and turns away, and a green ball makes it drive over. Unusually for this wave the description cites its sources - MaleCNS v1.0 from Janelia FlyEM (Berg et al., Cell 2026) for the wiring and Shiu et al. for the neuron model - so the claim is checkable rather than asserted.

items.title: A fruit fly's brain is driving this robot
items.author: Spranic

clusters.title: A fly nervous system flying a spaceship, with the aiming done for it
clusters.commentary: A 167,106-neuron MaleCNS v1.0 simulation is wired to movement and evasion in the game ORB1TAL: FRAGMENT. The studio states plainly that the fly does not aim or fire - the game handles weapons automatically - and that enemy drones are translated into visual threat stimuli, so what is on display is escape circuitry reacting to synthetic looming input rather than a fly playing a game.

items.title: A 167,106-Neuron Fly Brain Plays ORB1TAL: FRAGMENT
items.author: Malakaay Studios

clusters.title: The connectome chases a light, and loses at Pong
clusters.commentary: The male CNS wiring is set to chase a light source in a simulated room with no training, and the channel says it works - the circuit finds the light and closes on it. The same post reports that the identical circuit loses badly at Pong to a one-line if-statement. That negative result is the useful part: it is the clearest demonstration in this index that the connectome does the behaviour it evolved for and not the ones the game ports ask of it.

items.title: Real Fly Brain Chases a Light (No Training)
items.author: MuyunaLabs

clusters.title: Flycraft: a second fly brain in Minecraft
clusters.commentary: A separate Minecraft port from the one indexed above - a different author, a different build - with the source files offered on the creator's Patreon. The video does not state which connectome release it uses. Kept as its own entry because two people building the same kind of thing are two builds, not one.

items.title: I Used a Real Fly Brain to Control Minecraft
items.author: hacktic

clusters.title: Connectome-constrained vision benchmarked against CNNs
clusters.commentary: A NeurIPS 2026 spotlight paper, announced by one of its authors, benchmarking FlyNet - a connectome-constrained model of the Drosophila visual system - against CNNs, RAFT and an unconstrained recurrent network on a looming collision-detection task. The authors report it matches or beats those architectures on common perturbations at up to five orders of magnitude fewer FLOPs, while giving up some of the adversarial robustness the unconstrained network keeps. This is the connectome used as a modelling constraint rather than as a demo.

items.author: Srikanth Ramaswamy
items.text: Our paper 'Measuring Robustness and Efficiency in a Connectome-Constrained Fly Visual System Model on a Collision-Detection Task' has been selected as a Spotlight at NeurIPS 2026 ... we tested whether the fly's real synaptic wiring buys robustness, efficiency, or both.

clusters.title: The same simulated fly given alcohol, jobs and a reading test
clusters.commentary: Two more episodes of the ongoing series on what the creator describes as a 139,255-neuron scanned fly brain running in his own simulation: he says it gets drunk and finishes two of three jobs, and separately that given three screens and three keys it learned to read one picture in thirty seconds. Both learning claims are his. A wiring diagram carries no plasticity of its own, so whatever is changing lives in the simulation he built around it.

clusters.title: A MaleCNS model flying drones in Liftoff
clusters.commentary: A MaleCNS model flown in the drone simulator Liftoff: Micro Drones, framed by the creator as a fly that 'wakes up for 30 seconds at a time inside a drone'. The clip shows the flight, not the mapping from connectome output to control inputs, and it was posted the same day with 19 views, so nothing in it has been independently checked.

items.title: Fruit Fly Brain Male CNS in Liftoff: Micro Drones
items.author: Bryan Howard

clusters.title: Vinesauce streams Flyleno for half an hour
clusters.commentary: A 33-minute Vinesauce stream of Flyleno, a browser toy in which a fly-brain simulation pilots an on-screen character. It is a let's-play of someone else's build rather than a new simulation; what it demonstrates is the reach of the fly-brain wave into mainstream streaming, at roughly 42,000 views in two days.

clusters.title: A 150K-view reaction to the torturing-a-fruit-fly explainer
clusters.commentary: A 16-minute reaction video to Better Stack's 'The Internet Is Torturing a Fruit Fly' explainer, which is indexed here separately. There is no original build or analysis in it; it is included as a measure of how far that explainer travelled, at roughly 150,000 views in six days.

clusters.title: Connectome Atelier: the MaleCNS graph driving generative visuals
clusters.commentary: Billed as run 05 of a 'Connectome Atelier' series, in which the channel states the full 166,700-neuron MaleCNS v1.0 graph controlled the visual output. The clip is 14 seconds and shows only the result, so whether the connectome or the surrounding code produced the design is not checkable from the video.

items.title: Fruit Fly Designs WALL CONTACT | MaleCNS Run 05
items.author: husky

clusters.title: A fly brain steering a satellite in simulation
clusters.commentary: A connectome wired to a satellite attitude-control task, posted in Polish. Unusually careful framing for the genre: the author states up front that the fly is a digital map of its brain and that the satellite flew in simulation, and credits the FlyWire consortium with Princeton and Cambridge for the underlying data.

clusters.title: The connectome under a digital microscope
clusters.commentary: An interactive viewer that zooms from the whole fly down to individual neurons. The post states 139,255 neurons, 54.5 million synapses and 8,453 cell types, which are the FlyWire figures rather than MaleCNS. It visualizes the released data; it does not simulate it.

items.author: @insomnia_vip
items.text: I PUT AN ENTIRE FLY BRAIN UNDER A DIGITAL MICROSCOPE. Inside the model, it becomes an enormous network of connections with 139,255 neurons, 54.5 million synapses and 8,453 different cell types.

clusters.title: The same simulated fly made to play football and solve a maze
clusters.commentary: Two further episodes of the ongoing series on what the creator describes as a 139,255-neuron scanned fly brain running in his own simulation: 22 copies of it playing a game of football in which the losing team is deleted, and a single copy finding a lit cigarette at the centre of an 11x11 maze by smell, which he says took 46 seconds. As throughout the series, the simulator and the reward wiring are his own and are not shown.

items.text: I MADE 22 COPIES OF MY FLY PLAY FOOTBALL. THE LOSING TEAM DIED. one scanned fly brain, 139,255 neurons, copied 22 times, 11 red and 11 blue

items.author: @adamgrag
items.text: A fruit fly brain has 139,255 neurons and no idea what a map is. I dropped a real scanned one at the entrance of an 11x11 maze with a lit cigarette in the centre. It found it in 46 seconds.

clusters.title: The fly brain as a blueprint for neuromorphic hardware
clusters.commentary: A long-form post arguing that the fly connectome has become a benchmark for neuromorphic chips and embodied 'physical AI', working from how the brain was mapped through to how it is being run on hardware. Analysis rather than video, included on the same basis as the other explainer posts here; the hardware framing is the author's and no specific chip result is cited.

items.author: Rani M.
items.text: The Fly Brain as a Blueprint: Connectomics, Neuromorphic Computing, and Physical AI

clusters.title: A MaleCNS connectome playing Pokemon Emerald, live for three hours
clusters.commentary: A 2h48m live stream in which the MaleCNS v1.0 connectome, which the author gives as 166,700 neurons, is wired into Pokemon Emerald: the game screen is sampled through the model's photoreceptors and the buttons are pressed from its descending neurons. The author states the neurons are leaky integrate-and-fire units with constants from Shiu et al. (Nature, 2024), that the mushroom body is the only part that learns, and that no scripts or language model are involved. The on-screen panels show spiking activity, the dopamine signal and progress rungs, which is a readout of the simulation rather than evidence the fly understands the game.

items.title: Fruit fly connectome plays Pokemon Emerald | 166,700 simulated neurons, live
items.author: Mo
items.text: 166,700 neurons wired the way a real fly's are, getting the game screen through the fly's own photoreceptors and pressing buttons through its descending neurons. Wiring is MaleCNS v1.0 from Janelia/FlyEM; each neuron is a leaky integrate-and-fire unit with constants from Shiu et al. 2024. No scripts and no language model.

clusters.title: FlyCorp: four fly brains competing for three desks in MuJoCo
clusters.commentary: Episode seven of an ongoing series in which four copies of the FlyWire connectome, which the author gives as 138,639 simulated neurons each, drive office chairs in MuJoCo through the neurons that normally make a fly walk - P9 forward, MDN back, DNa02 for steering. The author says nothing is scripted and reports the trained brain reaching a desk roughly five times faster after thirty rounds of reward shaping, filmed at rounds 0, 15 and 30. The live panel plots every neuron at its mapped position as it spikes, so what is visible is connectome-derived activity steering a chair.

items.title: FlyCorp #7 The Reorg. 4 Fly Brains. 3 Desks. The Untrained Intern Kept His Job.
items.author: ipc0nfg
items.text: Four fruit fly brains (the FlyWire connectome, 138,639 simulated neurons each) drive office chairs in MuJoCo, seeing the office through their own simulated eyes. Desk school: 30 rounds, rewarded every 10 ms for getting closer to a desk. The exam: the trained brain got 5x faster to a desk.

clusters.title: A fly brain playing Gorilla Tag in VR
clusters.commentary: A VR channel's stunt video, 735,000 views in its first week, which says it taught a fly's open-source brain to move as a gorilla and play Gorilla Tag's infection mode across eight phases before the creator joins it in VR. Neither the video description nor the title names a dataset, a method or any code, so there is nothing to check the fly-brain claim against beyond the footage. It is both the highest-reach new item this run and the least documented one.

items.title: I Taught a Fly How to Play Gorilla Tag (seriously)
items.author: SuperCatCrazeGT
items.text: Using its open source brain, the fly learned to move around as a gorilla and got super good at it. It even learned how to play infection. In the end I actually play with it in VR.

clusters.title: Grey Leno: a talk show host puppeteered by a fly connectome
clusters.commentary: A browser-based late-night talk show whose host is driven by the FlyWire connectome, which the author gives as 138,639 neurons and 15.1M connections running from a 31MB file updated every 0.1ms. Unlike this account's earlier unsourced posts, the project ships as a public repo (github.com/SpikeCalls/grey-leno-fly-brain, JavaScript, created 2026-09-30) plus a live demo, so the claim that nobody writes the jokes or animates the body is at least inspectable. What it demonstrates is connectome-derived spiking driving a puppet rig, not comedy.

clusters.title: Shape sorter and colour sorting on a desktop fly brain
clusters.commentary: Two further episodes of the ongoing series on what the creator describes as a 139,255-neuron scanned fly brain running a body on his desk: a toddler's shape-sorter toy solved in 49 seconds, and ten balls sorted into same-coloured baskets, both rewarded with a cigarette box opening. His narration attributes deliberation to the fly - standing between the baskets rubbing its front legs, rolling a pyramid over after the square hole stops paying off - and the posts show neither the learning rule nor the simulator, so the behaviour is his account of it. The second post also notes that fruit flies are close to red-blind, which makes the red-versus-blue sorting the load-bearing claim of that episode.

clusters.title: One fly brain to mimic one rat neuron
clusters.commentary: A one-line claim with video from a computational neuroscientist: that one fly brain can almost perfectly mimic one rat neuron, which would put a whole fly connectome at roughly the compute needed to reproduce a single cortical neuron's input-output function. The post cites no paper, method or figures and has no thread behind it, so the comparison rests on the author's say-so; it is included because the claim is specific and comes from someone working in the field.

clusters.title: A world for the fly, with the connectome not yet plugged in
clusters.commentary: The fourth instalment of a FlyWire-based project built in public: a 3D room with drifting obstacles and glowing food in which a fly navigates autonomously. The author states plainly that the navigation is hand-coded ray-casting and angle-seeking rather than the spiking circuit from his earlier phases, and calls the environment a labelled placeholder built so the connectome-derived circuit has somewhere to be plugged in next. Worth indexing as the rare entry in this wave whose author says up front that the connectome is not driving what you are watching.

items.title: A visual milestone: the fly finally has a world to live in

items.text: Built a small 3D environment: a walled room, scattered obstacles, glowing food. Important honesty check: the fly's brain right now is simple hand-coded steering logic - ray-casting for obstacle avoidance, angle-seeking toward the nearest food. It is NOT yet driven by the actual spiking neural circuit from Phases 0-3.

clusters.title: The fly connectome as a latency problem, and then as an ASIC
clusters.commentary: An ASIC and FPGA engineer works out what it would cost to run the fly connectome at its real timing, reporting that even a coarse feed-forward approximation binning about 160,000 neurons into 122 bins comes to roughly 600M multiply-accumulates per step, and that the connectome's 2ms ingress-to-egress path with 0.1ms internal updates is beyond any GPU he can find or imagine. His follow-up moves the connectome logic to silicon instead, showing a SkyWater 130nm ASIC layout with a rough 50mW power estimate. Every figure is his own estimate from his own synthesis work; no benchmark, measurement or tapeout is shown.

items.title: Replicating the fly connectome with a feed-forward model, and why a GPU cannot keep up
items.author: Damir Wallener
items.text: I can roughly replicate the Fly connectome with a feed-forward LLM. 250k ish parameters, but 600M ish MACs is a problem when the fly is running at 0.1ms integration time, and the granularity is coarse: 160k neurons in 122 bins. The fly connectome has a 2ms cycle path. If we drop the AI model and build a chip to match the connectome, rough estimate is we can do it on 50mW.

clusters.title: A fly connectome ranking apartment listings
clusters.commentary: A FlyWire connectome, which the author gives as about 140,000 neurons and 54.5 million synapses, used to rank apartment listings in Limassol: hard filters run in ordinary code, then each listing photo is compressed to an 8x8 grid of 192 numbers and pushed through the connectome, with would-visit / maybe / not-for-me feedback shaping the ranking after a few examples. He states that the neuron positions, cell types and wiring come from published connectome data but the dynamics, input encoding and scoring are his own, and that the result proves nothing about how flies think. The demo shows activity propagating through real connectome neurons when a listing photo is clicked.

items.title: I hired a fly to find me an apartment in Limassol

items.author_title: Product Manager | AI agents, LLM applications & automation
items.text: Each apartment photo is compressed into an 8x8 grid, 192 numbers in total, and pushed through the connectome. I give it feedback: would visit, maybe, not for me. A necessary disclaimer: I am not simulating an actual fly. The dynamics, input encoding and the way neural activity becomes an apartment score are mine. This proves absolutely nothing about how flies think.

It is a counterpoint to the game ports and mind-uploading claims rather than a build of its own.

The author states the fly layer gets 25% of the final score, that a giant-fiber escape reflex can hard-block an action once learned valence drops below a set threshold, and that the reference graph is MaleCNS at 166,606 neurons and 25.5M edges. He is explicit that there are no spiking neurons and no claim to simulate a real fly, calling the system connectome-constrained rather than connectome-faithful.

items.title: The effect of fruit fly's brain neurons on LLM agent behaviour
items.author: Oppa AI
items.text: Currently doing research and test on the fly-brain neurons connectome as a biological simulation layer inside the brain of my local AI companion running on a Jetson Orin Nano. Modulatory only. The LLM proposes, the fly votes. The fly gets 25% of the final score. One veto: a giant fiber escape reflex can hard-block an external action, and only when learned valence drops below -0.6. Deliberately NOT included: spiking neurons, automatic weight tuning, or any claim of simulating a real fly. It's connectome-constrained, not connectome-faithful. The reference graph is MaleCNS (166,606 neurons, 25.5M edges).

clusters.title: A digital fly that looked like it followed light, and did not
clusters.commentary: A two-part build log: Mykola Bondarenko wires a simulated fruit-fly brain into a WebGL body with the goal of having a drone explore an unknown building, then reports that his own phototaxis result was an artifact — he states that almost every visual stimulus eventually produced the same saturated escape response. The follow-up describes building a headless twin of the environment and evolving the modelling parameters while leaving the connectome itself untouched. The creator debunking his own earlier clip is rarer than anything else in this index.

items.author: Mykola Bondarenko
items.text: What if a drone could explore an unknown building using a simulated fruit-fly brain instead of a traditional AI model? That is the experiment I'm building. [video: Can a Digital Fly Brain Explore ...]

items.author: Mykola Bondarenko
items.text: In my first experiment, I connected a digital fruit-fly brain to a virtual body and watched it climb toward the light. It looked surprisingly natural, and I assumed I was seeing phototaxis. I was wrong. When I started testing the brain directly, I discovered that almost every visual stimulus eventually produced essentially the same saturated escape response. That discovery changed the whole project. I built a headless twin of the WebGL environment, started evolving the modeling parameters without changing the connectome itself, and tried to answer a harder question: Can this fly actually explore an unknown room?

clusters.title: Asking a connectome which stripes a fly notices
clusters.commentary: Varun Reddy reports running 617 fabric patterns and 240 trap designs through an open-source model of the fly visual system, says it reproduced three results from live-fly experiments it was never given, and flags an apparently untested question: how wide the stripes on a fly trap should be. The post names neither the model nor the three results, so the reproduction claim is his and is not checked here; the appeal is that it asks the connectome a question with an answer outside it.

items.author: Varun Reddy
items.text: A fruit fly's visual system has been mapped synapse by synapse, and the model built on it is open source. I ran 617 fabric patterns and 240 trap designs through it. It reproduced three results from live-fly experiments it was never given — and pointed at a gap: nobody appears to have tested how wide the stripes on a fly trap should be.

The author made one wiring change, mirroring contralateral inputs to the motor neurons (0.6% of synapses), and reports that a placeholder controller, not an LLM, issues the commands; so far the body stands and takes one wobbly step.

items.author: @L_ARCH_01
items.text: Unreal EngineでLLMにボディを与えてみよう・その7 〜人型世界モデルと神経接続〜

clusters.title: The fly's escape reflex playing Geometry Dash
clusters.commentary: A FlyWire-based leaky integrate-and-fire model presses jump whenever its Giant Fiber escape neuron fires in response to a computed looming signal. The author reports 96% of 90 levels in his own clone, and 7 of 9 attempts past the opening spikes of the real Stereo Madness, against 0% with the Giant Fiber silenced or the wiring scrambled. He is specific about the limits: the input is a computed looming signal rather than pixels, and the obstacle layout comes from the level file.

items.author: Adithya CB
items.text: I wired one to Geometry Dash. It played without any training. Then I found exactly where a reflex stops being enough.

clusters.title: Swat the fly: a browser game with a shuffled-wiring control
clusters.commentary: A playable browser game where you try to swat a fly whose brain is 5,555 neurons from the MaleCNS connectome; looming detectors drive the escape neuron, and a replay shows the spikes on real neuron shapes. The author's experiment is the more useful part: shuffled wiring first looked dramatically different (about 120 spikes/s per neuron versus 2.7), but a stricter shuffle that preserves each neuron's total input brought it to 4.4, which he reports as not significant.

items.author: Alpar Arman
items.text: I made 499 copies of the brain where every neuron keeps the same number of connections, but the partners are shuffled.

clusters.title: A fly-wired controller for a simulated robot arm in a greenhouse
clusters.commentary: 4,476 FlyWire neurons used as the controller for a simulated Panda arm in MuJoCo, trained with PPO. The author reports about 98% on single-step tasks such as harvesting a ripe tomato, falling to 67-72% on multi-step truss clearing against 98% for a scripted teacher, and says the video shows solved attempts only.

items.author: S. M. Nihal Ahmed
items.text: Can a fruit fly's brain run a robot arm? I took the wiring of a real fruit fly brain (the FlyWire connectome, 4,476 neurons) and used it as the controller for a simulated Panda robot arm in MuJoCo.

clusters.title: A student robot that backs away from looming objects using fly escape neurons
clusters.commentary: A university module project: a model of the fly's visual lobe is mapped neuron by neuron onto the MaleCNS connectome, and walking, steering and escape neuron activity is translated into motor commands every 20 ms. The team reports their motion-detecting neurons are a median 9 degrees off what the wiring predicts, and that the robot retreats from dark looming objects with no object detection in the code.

items.author: Ilia Mirzaali
items.text: For our module project we gave a fly's brain its own physical body

clusters.title: They lied to you about the virtual fly brain (10 Physics)
clusters.commentary: A short corrective explainer aimed at the viral wave: the creator argues that many online claims about the fruit fly connectome are exaggerated, and points viewers to Virtual Fly Brain and the 2024 FlyWire Nature papers. At about 419,000 views it is one of the few widely watched pushbacks in this index.

items.title: They Lied to you about the Virtual Fly Brain
items.author: 10 Physics

clusters.title: A biophysical simulation of the fly's visual system
clusters.commentary: Liu Ziyin and colleagues biophysically simulated the visual system from the Drosophila connectome and report that it detects small objects moving against a noisy background through subcellular interactions between one large inhibitory cell and a pool of small cells (bioRxiv preprint). The clip is a simplified visualisation of that simulation, not the full model.

items.author: @LiuZiyin10
items.text: How to model a brain given its full anatomy? We took the Drosophila connectome and biophysically simulated its visual system.

clusters.title: One sexually dimorphic neuron type, male versus female (Janelia)
clusters.commentary: A 56-second Janelia visualisation of AOTU012, a neuron type present in both sexes that connects to different partners in each, comparing male CNS data with the female FlyWire data. It illustrates the male-versus-female comparison that the MaleCNS release made possible; it predates the September viral wave by about a year.

items.title: Sexual dimorphism in the fruit fly central nervous system
items.author: HHMI's Janelia Research Campus

clusters.title: A fly connectome flying a quadcopter, weights released
clusters.commentary: Singularity Edge wired a fruit fly connectome into a four-rotor drone controller and released the model, weights and code on Hugging Face as FlyDrone-SNN. They report that training changed only 1.7% of the connectome's weights, with a median change of zero, and that deleting that 1.7% makes the drone crash; their reading is that the wiring was already most of the flight algorithm. The 138,000-neuron count and the 0.5-1 W neuromorphic power figure are theirs, and the claim is about their own training setup, not a measurement of a living fly.

items.author: Jan Miran K.
items.title: We took the actual connectome of a fruit fly and wired it directly into a 4-motor drone

clusters.title: FlyDrive: a car that brakes with the fly's escape neurons
clusters.commentary: A side project that routes a driving simulator's emergency braking and swerving through the FlyWire connectome's looming detectors and escape neurons, run as a spiking network on CPU. The video is a lesion comparison: with ten escape neurons silenced the hand-tuned controller hit 27 of 29 obstacles against 6 when intact, while a reinforcement-learned version was unaffected because it had found other routes through the network. The author reports 93% obstacle avoidance, notes that retraining on camera pixels gave no safety gain, and calls it a toy rather than a self-driving car.

items.author: Pradeepkrishna G.
items.title: FlyDrive: emergency reflexes on the fly's complete connectome

clusters.title: How Janelia got to a whole fly brain
clusters.commentary: HHMI's own retrospective on the Janelia fly connectomics programme, which it dates to a 2008 decision to build a complete wiring diagram. Institutional history rather than new data, and the clearest short answer to why the 2026 releases exist at all.

items.title: The History of Fruit Fly Connectomics at Janelia
items.author: Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI)

clusters.title: The FlyWire reconstruction as pure geometry
clusters.commentary: A scientific visualization studio's 3D render of the FlyWire reconstruction, which the video puts at over 139,000 neurons. No simulation and no behaviour, just the shape of the data; it predates the 2026 wave and is the kind of render the viral builds are layered on top of.

items.title: 3D reconstruction of the fruit fly brain connectome. Over 139,000 neurons
items.author: Quorumetrix Studio

clusters.title: About that brain they uploaded
clusters.commentary: A three-minute correction to the uploaded-fly framing around Eon Systems' walking model: the video points out that Eon's own write-up attributes the walking to pre-trained body controllers, with the connectome contributing only a few high-level signals. It cites the FlyWire map at 139,255 neurons and 54.5 million synapses, and lands on the map being real while the walking was rehearsed.

items.title: About That Brain They Uploaded
items.author: Control Group - Three Minute Science

clusters.title: A simulated fly living in a painting, streaming 24/7
clusters.commentary: A continuous real-time stream in which a fruit fly walks, grooms and flies around a Morandi-style still life rendered in Godot, with its behaviour driven by a connectome simulation the creator says runs 165,122 neurons from the male central nervous system data. The description is unusually careful about its own limits, stating that the on-screen hunger and mood meters are a game layer rather than biology and that the stream is not evidence of learning in a living brain. It is a new channel with a handful of concurrent viewers, so the simulation's fidelity is the creator's claim and is not independently shown.

items.title: The fly brain - Cozy 24/7 Living Painting · A Simulated Fly Lives Here · Real-Time
items.author: Lord of the Flies

items.title: The fly brain - Cozy 24/7 Living Painting · A Simulated Fly Lives Here · Real-Time
items.author: Lord of the Flies

clusters.title: A fly's looming-and-escape circuit on a $5 chip
clusters.commentary: A hobbyist build that runs 48,311 neurons of the fruit fly connectome on a $5 ESP32-S3 and lets the wiring decide when, and which way, a virtual fly escapes an approaching ball. The creator reports that the whole-brain version needs 1.6 seconds per step, far too slow to dodge in real time, and that cutting it down to 319 neurons - the looming detectors and the escape neurons - brings a decision to 2.2 milliseconds. Both timings are his own measurements on his own rig, and the escape is a reflex arc rather than anything learned.

items.title: I Put a Real Fly's Brain in a Virtual Body
items.author: Fit & Predict

clusters.title: A fly-brain Minecraft agent that barely worked
clusters.commentary: Another Minecraft build, wiring synthetic eyes to a fruit fly brain model, giving it a goal and posting the code on GitHub. The creator's own title says it barely worked, and the only figure offered is an 11.33-point gain in success rate over his initial tests, which measures his agent against its own earlier runs rather than against any standard baseline.

items.title: I Taught a Fruit Fly Brain to Play Minecraft (It Barely Worked)
items.author: NotMuchBytes

clusters.title: Fly descending neurons made to moonwalk a 3D mouse
clusters.commentary: A demo from the Annolid tool project in which a 264-neuron spiking model, drawn from male-cns v1.0, FlyWire and MANC sensorimotor pathways, drives a rigged 3D mouse in a Three.js simulation, with a simulated optogenetic pulse to the moonwalker descending neuron sending it backwards. The fly circuitry is a small hand-picked subset driving an animated mouse through a four-limb pattern generator, so it demonstrates a pathway wired to a rig, not a simulation of either animal.

items.title: A Fruit Fly Brain Makes a 3D Mouse Moonwalk! | Annolid NeuroAI Demo
items.author: Annolid

clusters.title: Looking for a simulated fly's internal state in its photoreceptors
clusters.commentary: Part of a series the creator calls Cognesia: he loads the FlyWire wiring, which he gives as 138,639 neurons and 54 million synapses, into a simulator built at Synoch and models membrane potentials while the fly watches a moving stripe in three internal states. He reports photoreceptors sitting about 0.76 mV higher when hungry than when well-fed with an unchanged peak, and states plainly that each state was run once and not under identical conditions, so the difference cannot yet be pinned on chemistry. The title's question about lying is not what the experiment tests.

items.title: Can I Make a Fruit Fly Lie?
items.author: Synoch

clusters.title: ConnectomeToBehaviour: altering the wiring to see what behaviour does
clusters.commentary: An open-source project putting the FlyWire central-brain connectome into a spiking network attached to a simulated body, with the stated aim of studying how changes to the wiring affect the model's behaviour. The author describes it as still ongoing and links the repository rather than results, so what is on offer is the setup and the code, not a finding.

items.author: @visionbyangelic
items.text: Still Ongoing: ConnectomeToBehaviour. I am using the FlyWire connectome of the fruit fly's central brain in a spiking network model connected to a simulated body, to study how changes to the wiring affect the model's behaviour.

clusters.title: A whole FlyWire brain as a decision engine, with predictions written down first (makerATL)
clusters.commentary: A four-minute summary of a hobby study that runs the Shiu et al. spiking model of all 138,639 FlyWire neurons as a smell-to-decision engine, with home-made fish and tunnel bodies, a retina and a decoder bolted on. The maker says each experiment's prediction was recorded before it was run and that wrong ones were kept, including a case where the model learned the wrong thing. The description credits Claude Code with writing and running the experiments and labels the narration as synthetic, so this is a documented case study, not peer-reviewed work.

items.title: Simulating a fruit fly’s whole brain: 138,639 neurons making decisions (FlyWire connectome)
items.author: makerATL

clusters.title: The MaleCNS nervous system grown one neuron at a time
clusters.commentary: A 28-second render that draws each MaleCNS v1.0 neuron along its traced shape inside a glass fly, in signal order: sensory neurons, optic lobes, central brain, descending neurons, nerve cord. The description says the order was chosen for clarity and is not how a fly brain develops, and that the closing spikes come from the creator's own smell simulation shown about 500 times slower than real time.

items.title: Every neuron of a fruit fly brain, built one by one
items.author: The Consciousness Research

clusters.title: Five senses arriving in the MaleCNS nervous system
clusters.commentary: A 29-second render that starts the sensory neurons of smell, taste, touch, sound and light in turn and follows the spikes along the traced fibres as each set of neurons fires the next. The creator puts the wiring at 165,122 traced neurons from MaleCNS v1.0, of which 49,759 were drawn, and credits the mapping to HHMI Janelia with Cambridge, the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology and Google Research. It shows propagation through measured anatomy, not a fly perceiving anything.

items.title: Watch a fruit fly brain fire, spike by spike
items.author: The Consciousness Research

clusters.title: A target-tracking controller wired from connectome subgraphs
clusters.commentary: A university course project, credited to an AI course group at NCKU and CCU, presenting a multisensory tracking system whose recurrent controller is taken from connectome wiring rather than learned from scratch. The description specifies an 8,792-neuron, 185,261-edge subgraph of MaleCNS v1.0 linking lobula columnar visual neurons, olfactory receptor neurons and Johnston's-organ wind sensors to the descending neurons that set forward speed and turning, trained by imitation on top of a frozen flyvis front end. Every figure here is the team's own.

items.title: A Multisensory Bio-Inspired Target Tracking System Based on Drosophila Neural Circuits
items.author: F74

clusters.title: Flyuigi: a second fly brain put in charge of Super Mario Bros
clusters.commentary: A separate Super Mario build from the one already in this index, by a different creator. The game state is turned into sensory input, MaleCNS v1.0 neurons fire, and that activity presses the buttons; the creator states the wiring is never touched and that evolution only tunes how strongly each sense is weighted. A browser demo and the source are both published, so the setup can be inspected. The claim of clearing World 1-1 ten times out of ten is the creator's.

items.title: I put a real fruit fly’s brain in charge of Super Mario Bros
items.author: codeRun

clusters.title: An explainer on what the fly upload actually was
clusters.commentary: A nine-minute explainer that walks from the C. elegans wiring diagram to the roughly 140,000-neuron fruit fly reconstruction and then asks whether a human brain could be treated the same way. Its own description says the virtual fly walks, grooms and eats, and flags a significant caveat behind that. The title's claim that the first animal brain has been uploaded and that humans are next is the video's framing, not a result.

items.title: Scientists Just Uploaded the First Animal Brain, and Humans Are Next
items.author: Dan Grib

clusters.title: A connectome fly loose in a real room, through AR glasses
clusters.commentary: An augmented-reality build by Pavlo Tkachenko that places a virtual fly in a real room through Snap Spectacles. The creator describes the loop as the glasses' camera, rays and hand tracking feeding sense channels into the MaleCNS connectome, whose descending and motor neurons drive the fly's wings, legs and head. The clip shows the result, not how the sensory and motor mappings were built.

items.author: @pt_pavlo
items.text: A fly that is a fly, its own connectome brain, perceiving the real room through its own senses with power of AR now have digital 🪰 Flow: Spectacles(retina + rays + hands) → (room inventory) → sense channels → MaleCNS brain → DNs + motor pools → Specstacles → wings, legs, head

items.author: @Ronald_vanLoon
items.text: Meet the #Digital Fly: A Connectome Brain Experiencing the Real World Through #AR by @pt_pavlo

clusters.title: A simulated fly brain's spikes turned into a song
clusters.commentary: A clip from the @malecnsfly account that sets spikes from a simulated fly brain to music, with lyrics the creator writes. The creator says every note is a real spike and none is altered; the post does not say how spikes were mapped to notes, so this is a sonification, not something the fly composed.

items.author: @malecnsfly
items.text: last night, his brain sang. 🪰 every note is a real spike. i don't change a single one. i only write the words. first line: "i have no voice, so i borrowed yours."

clusters.title: Relaying Rubik's cube moves through a fly's visual system
clusters.commentary: A build that shows a cube solver's moves, through the creator's own glasses, to the retina of a spiking MaleCNS v1.0 model and reads each move back out of the medulla. The creator reports 305 of 306 moves relayed and 7 of 8 scrambles solved, and states that the fly learned nothing, that the move decoding is a lookup table they built, and that its motor neurons never fired. It shows a visual signal surviving the first couple of synapses, not a fly solving a cube.

items.title: MaleCNS v1.0 fly brain simulation: 305 of 306 cube moves relayed
items.author: Sidequest Maker

clusters.title: A long explainer on Eon's fly and the MaleCNS release
clusters.commentary: A 17-minute explainer that runs from Eon's March 2026 claim to have uploaded a fruit fly to the September 2026 MaleCNS release, framed around AI tracing neurons from microscope images. Its description says every claim comes from published research and reporting. "Uploaded" is Eon's word, and the video's line that AI is starting to run brains is its framing, not a result.

items.title: The First Brain Was Just Uploaded To A Computer
items.author: There's An AI For That

clusters.title: How the fly brain got out, and whether a copy can suffer
clusters.commentary: An explainer that runs from the 302-neuron worm wired into a Lego robot, through the fly brain traced from thousands of electron-microscope slices, to the September 2026 release that people put into Minecraft, Doom and Beat Saber, and ends on whether a copied brain could feel anything. The figure that a whole-brain simulation predicted real neurons nine times out of ten is the video's summary of earlier published work.

items.title: This Fly Is Being Tortured Inside the Internet
items.author: Not Hypothetical

clusters.title: Srini Turaga on connectome-constrained whole-body fly simulation
clusters.commentary: A workshop talk by Srini Turaga of HHMI Janelia at the NeuroAgents workshop on working toward simulations of whole-body fruit fly behaviour constrained by the connectome. It is a research talk on methods and goals, separate from his longer FlyComp2025 lecture already in this index.

items.title: Srini Turaga (Janelia) - Connectome-constrained simulation of whole-body fruit fly behavior
items.author: NeuroAgents Workshop
